pumac-2015-power-01a.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-01a.body: Subtraction is not associative: $4-(2-7)=9\ne-5=(4-2)-7$. (Also there is no two-sided identity.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-01b.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-01b.body: There is no identity element ($0\notin\mathbb N$), and no element has an additive inverse (e.g. $2$ has none in $\mathbb N$). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-01c.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-01c.body: The element $0$ has no multiplicative inverse: $0\cdot x=0\ne1$ for all $x$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-01d.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-01d.body: The product of nonzero rationals is a nonzero rational (closed); multiplication is associative; $1$ is the identity; and $\frac pq\cdot\frac qp=1$ gives inverses. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-02.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-02.body:
*Closed:* if $a,b
ot\equiv0\pmod p$ then $p
mid ab$ ($p$ is prime), so $ab
ot\equiv0$. *Associative, commutative, identity $1$:* inherited from $\mathbb Z$. *Inverses:* if $a
ot\equiv0$, then $\gcd(a,p)=1$ since $p$ is prime, so by Bézout there are $m,n$ with $ma+np=1$, i.e. $am\equiv1\pmod p$ and $m
ot\equiv0$. So $a^{-1}=m$ exists. $ lacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-03.title: Pigeonhole
pumac-2015-power-03.body: The powers $g,g^2,g^3,\dots$ lie in the finite set $G$, so $g^i=g^j$ for some $i>j\ge1$. Multiplying by $(g^{-1})^j$ gives $g^{i-j}=e$ with $i-j>0$. So the order of $g$ is finite. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-04.title: Derive the axioms
pumac-2015-power-04.body: Pick $a\in H$. Taking $a=b$ gives $e=aa^{-1}\in H$. For $b\in H$, taking $a=e$ gives $b^{-1}=eb^{-1}\in H$. For $a,b\in H$, $b^{-1}\in H$ so $ab=a(b^{-1})^{-1}\in H$: $H$ is closed. Associativity is inherited from $G$, $e\in H$ is the identity of $H$ and inverses lie in $H$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-05.title: Cosets
pumac-2015-power-05.body:
Let $H\le G$ be a subgroup. The left cosets $xH=\{xh:h\in H\}$ all have $|H|$ elements (since $h\mapsto xh$ is injective), every $x\in G$ lies in the coset $xH$ (as $e\in H$), and two cosets are equal or disjoint: if $z\in xH\cap yH$, $z=xh_1=yh_2$, then $x=yh_2h_1^{-1}$ and $xH=yh_2h_1^{-1}H=yH$. So $G$ is a disjoint union of cosets, each of size $|H|$, and $|H|$ divides $|G|=n$.

Apply this to $H=\langle g\rangle=\{e,g,\dots,g^{l-1}\}$ where $l$ is the order of $g$ (finite by 3.3): this is a subgroup (closed under products and inverses since $g^l=e$) with exactly $l$ elements (the powers $g^0,\dots,g^{l-1}$ are distinct, otherwise $g^i=g^j$ with $0<i-j<l$ gives a smaller exponent). Hence $l\mid n$, $n=lm$, and $g^n=(g^l)^m=e$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-06.title: Both directions
pumac-2015-power-06.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $g$ have odd order $m$, and $t=\frac{m+1}2$ (an integer). Put $h_k=g^{t^k}$. Then $h_k^{2^k}=g^{(2t)^k}=g^{(m+1)^k}=g$, because $(m+1)^k\equiv1\pmod m$ and $g^m=e$.

($\Leftarrow$) Write $|G|=2^s x$ with $x$ odd and take $k=s$: there is $h$ with $h^{2^s}=g$. Then $g^x=h^{2^sx}=h^{|G|}=e$ by Lagrange's theorem (3.5). So the order of $g$ divides the odd number $x$, hence is odd. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-07a.title: Depress the cubic
pumac-2015-power-07a.body: Take $m=1$, $n=-\frac{a_2}3$, i.e. $x=x'-\frac{a_2}3$. Then $x^3+a_2x^2=x'^3-a_2x'^2+\frac{a_2^2}3x'-\frac{a_2^3}{27}+a_2x'^2-\frac{2a_2^2}3x'+\frac{a_2^3}9$, in which the $x'^2$ terms cancel, so $f=x'^3+b_1x'+b_0$ with $b_1=a_1-\frac{a_2^2}3$ and $b_0=a_0-\frac{a_1a_2}3+\frac{2a_2^3}{27}$, both rational. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-07b.title: Three changes of variables
pumac-2015-power-07b.body:
**1. Complete the square.** Put $y=\frac12(Y-a_1x-a_3)$. Then $y^2+(a_1x+a_3)y=\frac14\bigl(Y^2-(a_1x+a_3)^2\bigr)$, so $E$ becomes $Y^2=4x^3+b_2x^2+b_4x+b_6$ with $b_2=a_1^2+4a_2$, $b_4=2a_4+a_1a_3$, $b_6=a_3^2+4a_6$ (integers).
**2. Make the cubic monic.** Multiply by $16$: $(4Y)^2=(4x)^3+b_2(4x)^2+4b_4(4x)+16b_6$. With $u=4x$, $v=4Y$: $v^2=u^3+b_2u^2+4b_4u+16b_6$.
**3. Remove the $u^2$ term.** Put $u=u'-\frac{b_2}3$ (Problem 4.1(a)): $v^2=u'^3+A_0u'+B_0$ with rational $A_0,B_0$.
**4. Clear denominators.** Choose $N\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $N^4A_0,N^6B_0\in\mathbb Z$ (e.g. $N=3$ times anything needed). Multiply by $N^6$: $(N^3v)^2=(N^2u')^3+A_0N^4(N^2u')+B_0N^6$. With $x'=N^2u'$, $y'=N^3v$ we get $y'^2=x'^3+Ax'+B$ with $A=N^4A_0$, $B=N^6B_0\in\mathbb Z$.
The composition is an invertible change of variables $(x,y)\mapsto(x',y')$ (rational coefficients). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-08a.title: Chord through the two points
pumac-2015-power-08a.body: The line through $(6,-9)$ and $(-4,1)$ has slope $\frac{1+9}{-4-6}=-1$: $y=-x-3$. Substituting, $(x+3)^2=x^3-20x-15$, i.e. $x^3-x^2-26x-24=0$; the roots are $6,-4$ and (by Vieta, sum $=1$) $x=1-6+4=-1$, with $y=-(-1)-3=-2$. So $(6,-9)*(-4,1)=(-1,-2)$ and the sum is its reflection $(-1,2)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-08b.title: Chord formula
pumac-2015-power-08b.body: Slope $m=\frac{2913-9}{204-6}=\frac{2904}{198}=\frac{44}3$. The third intersection has $x=m^2-6-204=\frac{1936}9-210=\frac{46}9$ and $y=9+m\bigl(\frac{46}9-6\bigr)=9-\frac{352}{27}=-\frac{109}{27}$. The sum is the reflection: $\left(\frac{46}9,\frac{109}{27}\right)$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-09a.title: Vieta
pumac-2015-power-09a.body:
The line $PQ$ is $y=\lambda x+
u$ with $\lambda= rac{d-b}{c-a}$, $
u=b-\lambda a$ rational. Substituting into $y^2=x^3+Ax+B$ gives $x^3-\lambda^2x^2+(A-2\lambda
u)x+(B-
u^2)=0$, whose roots include $a$ and $c$. By Vieta the third root is $x_3=\lambda^2-a-c\in\mathbb Q$, and then $y_3=\lambda x_3+
u\in\mathbb Q$. So $P*Q=(x_3,y_3)$ is rational and so is its reflection $P+Q=(x_3,-y_3)$. $ lacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-09b.title: Cayley–Bacharach
pumac-2015-power-09b.body:
Work in the projective plane; $O=(0:1:0)$ is the point at infinity, and the vertical lines are the lines through $O$. For a point $T\in E$ the vertical line through $T$ meets $E$ again at $-T$ (reflection), so $P+Q=-(P*Q)$.

Let $R_1=P*Q$, $S_1=P+Q=-R_1$, $R_2=Q*H$, $S_2=Q+H=-R_2$. Consider the lines
$$\ell_1=PQ\ (\ni R_1),\quad \ell_2=\text{vertical line }OR_2S_2,\quad \ell_3=HS_1\ (\ni X:=H*S_1),$$
$$m_1=QH\ (\ni R_2),\quad m_2=\text{vertical line }OR_1S_1,\quad m_3=PS_2\ (\ni Y:=P*S_2).$$
The cubics $C=\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3$ and $C'=m_1m_2m_3$ meet in the nine points $\ell_i\cap m_j$:
$$\ell_1\cap m_1=Q,\ \ell_1\cap m_2=R_1,\ \ell_1\cap m_3=P,\ \ell_2\cap m_1=R_2,\ \ell_2\cap m_2=O,\ \ell_2\cap m_3=S_2,\ \ell_3\cap m_1=H,\ \ell_3\cap m_2=S_1,\ \ell_3\cap m_3=:Z.$$
The first eight lie on $E$. By Cayley–Bacharach $E$ (a cubic) passes through the ninth point $Z$ as well. Now $Z$ lies on the line $\ell_3=HS_1$ and on $E$, and this line meets $E$ in exactly $H,S_1,X$; since $Z$ differs from $H,S_1$ (the nine points are distinct) we get $Z=X$. Similarly $Z$ lies on $m_3=PS_2$, which meets $E$ in $P,S_2,Y$, so $Z=Y$. Hence $X=Y$, i.e. $H*(P+Q)=P*(Q+H)$. Reflecting,
$$(P+Q)+H=-(S_1*H)=-X=-Y=-(P*S_2)=P+(Q+H).\ \blacksquare$$

pumac-2015-power-10.title: $p$-adic valuations
pumac-2015-power-10.body:
Let $p$ be a prime, $\beta=v_p(b)$, $\delta=v_p(d)$, so $v_p(x)=v_p(a/b)=-\beta$ if $\beta>0$ and $v_p(y)=-\delta$ if $\delta>0$ (coordinates in lowest terms), and $v_p(x),v_p(y)\ge0$ otherwise. The equation is $y^2+(e_1x+e_3)y=x^3+e_2x^2+e_4x+e_6$.

* If $\beta>0$: the right side has valuation exactly $-3\beta$ (the cubic term dominates). On the left, $v_p(y^2)=-2\delta$ and $v_p((e_1x+e_3)y)\ge-\beta-\delta$. If $\delta\le\beta$ both are $>-3\beta$ (as $-2\delta\ge-2\beta$ and $-\beta-\delta\ge-2\beta$), a contradiction. So $\delta>\beta$; then $-2\delta<-\beta-\delta$ and the left side has valuation exactly $-2\delta$, giving $2\delta=3\beta$.
* If $\beta=0$ and $\delta>0$: the left side has valuation $-2\delta<0$ ($y^2$ dominates $(e_1x+e_3)y$, of valuation $\ge-\delta$) while the right side has valuation $\ge0$: impossible.
* If $\beta=\delta=0$ nothing to prove.
Hence $2v_p(d)=3v_p(b)$ for every prime $p$, so $d^2=b^3$ (positive integers). (Equivalently $b=e^2$, $d=e^3$ for an integer $e$.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-11a.title: Roots of $y^2+y=\text{const}$
pumac-2015-power-11a.body: For fixed $x=a$, $y$ satisfies $y^2+y=a^3-a$, a quadratic with sum of roots $-1$. So the other root is $c=-1-b$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-11b.title: Midpoint
pumac-2015-power-11b.body: By part (a) the points $(a,b)$ and $(a,-1-b)$ are the reflections of each other, so the line of symmetry is $y=\frac{b+(-1-b)}2=-\frac12$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-12.title: Invariant plus induction
pumac-2015-power-12.body:
All $a_n$ are positive rationals (indeed integers, by 5.2), so no denominator below vanishes. Write $u=a_{n-1},v=a_n,w=a_{n+1},z=a_{n+2}$ and
$$G_n=u^2z^2-4uvwz+uw^3+v^3z+v^2w^2,\qquad R_n=(x_n,y_n)=\Bigl(\tfrac{v^2-uw}{v^2},\ \tfrac{u^2z-2uvw}{v^3}\Bigr).$$

**Step 1: $G_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$.** $G_1=1-4+1+1+1=0$ (all four terms equal $1$). For the step, with $r=a_{n+3}$ and $ur=zv+w^2$ (the recurrence), expanding shows
$$u\,G_{n+1}=r\,G_n,$$
where $G_{n+1}=v^2r^2-4vwzr+vz^3+w^3r+w^2z^2$. (Substitute $r=(zv+w^2)/u$ and multiply by $u^2$: both sides become the same polynomial $u^2G_{n+1}=(zv+w^2)G_n$; this is a direct expansion.) As $u\ne0$, $G_n=0\Rightarrow G_{n+1}=0$.

**Step 2: induction on $n$.** *Base:* $R_1=\bigl(\frac{1-1}1,\frac{1\cdot a_3-2}1\bigr)=(0,-1)=-P$ ✓, which is $(2\cdot1-3)P$. *Step:* assume $(2n-3)P=R_n$. Put $Q=2P=(1,0)$. Since $x_n-1=-\frac{uw}{v^2}\ne0$, the line through $R_n$ and $Q$ is non-vertical with slope $m=\frac{y_n}{x_n-1}=-\frac{uz-2vw}{vw}$. Substituting $y=m(x-1)$ into $y^2+y=x^3-x$ gives a cubic in $x$ with $x^3-m^2x^2+\dots$ whose roots are $x_n$, $1$ and the third root $x_T=m^2-1-x_n$. Now
$$m^2-1-x_n=\frac{(uz-2vw)^2}{v^2w^2}-2+\frac{uw}{v^2}\quad\text{and}\quad x_{n+1}=1-\frac{vz}{w^2},$$
and the difference $x_T-x_{n+1}$, after putting everything over $v^2w^2$, is $\frac{(uz-2vw)^2-3v^2w^2+uw^3+v^3z}{v^2w^2}=\frac{G_n}{v^2w^2}=0$. So $x_T=x_{n+1}$. For the $y$-coordinate of the third point $T$ of the line: $y_T=m(x_{n+1}-1)=\frac{uz-2vw}{vw}\cdot\frac{vz}{w^2}=\frac{z(uz-2vw)}{w^3}$. We must check $y_T=-1-y_{n+1}$, where $y_{n+1}=\frac{v^2a_{n+3}-2vwz}{w^3}$ and $a_{n+3}=\frac{zv+w^2}u$. This is equivalent to $w^3y_T+w^3+v^2a_{n+3}-2vwz=0$, i.e. $z(uz-2vw)+w^3+\frac{v^2(zv+w^2)}u-2vwz=0$; multiplying by $u$,
$$u^2z^2-4uvwz+uw^3+v^3z+v^2w^2=G_n=0.$$
Hence $T=(x_{n+1},-1-y_{n+1})=-R_{n+1}$. Therefore $R_n+Q=-T=R_{n+1}$, i.e. $(2n-3)P+2P=(2n-1)P=(2(n+1)-3)P=R_{n+1}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-13a.title: Direct computation
pumac-2015-power-13a.body:
Write $a=a_{n-3}$, $b=a_{n-2}$, $c=a_{n-1}$, $d=a_n$, $e=a_{n+1}$, $f=a_{n+2}$, $g=a_{n+3}$, $h=a_{n-4}$. The recurrences at indices $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$ read
$$dh=ca+b^2,\qquad ea=db+c^2,\qquad fb=ec+d^2,\qquad gc=fd+e^2.$$
Also $s_{n-1}=hf-ae$ and $s_n=ag-bf$. Then
$$a_n^2s_{n-1}-a_{n-1}^2s_n=d^2(hf-ae)-c^2(ag-bf)=f(d^2h+c^2b)-a(d^2e+c^2g).$$
Use $d^2h=d(ca+b^2)$ and $c^2g=c(fd+e^2)$:
$$=f(dca+db^2+c^2b)-a(d^2e+cfd+ce^2)=fb\,(db+c^2)-ae\,(d^2+ce)=fb\cdot ae-ae\cdot fb=0,$$
using $db+c^2=ea$ and $d^2+ce=fb$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-13b.title: Induction
pumac-2015-power-13b.body: Base $n=1$: $s_1=a_{-2}a_4-a_{-1}a_3=3\cdot2-2\cdot1=4=4a_1^2$. Step: if $s_{n-1}=4a_{n-1}^2$, then by (a) (all $a_k$ positive) $s_n=\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n-1}^2}s_{n-1}=4a_n^2$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-14.title: Strong induction
pumac-2015-power-14.body:
Base: $a_0,\dots,a_5=1,1,1,1,2,3$ are integers, and consecutive terms and terms two apart are coprime.

Let $m\ge6$ and assume $a_0,\dots,a_{m-1}$ are positive integers with $\gcd(a_k,a_{k-1})=\gcd(a_k,a_{k-2})=1$ for $k<m$.

*Integrality.* The recurrence gives $a_ma_{m-4}=a_{m-1}a_{m-3}+a_{m-2}^2\in\mathbb Z$, and $5.1(b)$ with $n=m-3$ gives $a_ma_{m-6}=4a_{m-3}^2+a_{m-5}a_{m-1}\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\gcd(a_{m-4},a_{m-6})=1$ there are integers $r,s$ with $ra_{m-4}+sa_{m-6}=1$, hence $a_m=r(a_ma_{m-4})+s(a_ma_{m-6})\in\mathbb Z$; it is positive.

*Coprimality.* If a prime $p$ divides $a_m$ and $a_{m-1}$, the recurrence $a_ma_{m-4}=a_{m-1}a_{m-3}+a_{m-2}^2$ gives $p\mid a_{m-2}^2$, so $p\mid a_{m-2}$, contradicting $\gcd(a_{m-1},a_{m-2})=1$. If $p$ divides $a_m$ and $a_{m-2}$, then $p\mid a_{m-1}a_{m-3}$; but $p\nmid a_{m-1}$ (as $\gcd(a_{m-1},a_{m-2})=1$) and $p\nmid a_{m-3}$ (as $\gcd(a_{m-2},a_{m-3})=1$), a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-15.title: Pure periodicity
pumac-2015-power-15.body: Fix $n>1$ and consider $f:(\mathbb Z/n)^3\to(\mathbb Z/n)^3$, $f(x,y,z)=(y,z,yz+x)$, so $f(b_i,b_{i+1},b_{i+2})=(b_{i+1},b_{i+2},b_{i+3})$. $f$ is a bijection: its inverse is $(x,y,z)\mapsto(z-xy,x,y)$. A bijection of a finite set has finite order $T\ge1$, so $f^T(1,1,1)=(1,1,1)$ modulo $n$. Now $f(0,1,1)=(1,1,1\cdot1+0)=(1,1,1)$. Hence $f(f^{T-1}(1,1,1))=f^T(1,1,1)=(1,1,1)=f(0,1,1)$, and injectivity of $f$ gives $f^{T-1}(1,1,1)=(0,1,1)$. But $f^{T-1}(1,1,1)=(b_{T-1},b_T,b_{T+1})\bmod n$. Therefore $b_{T-1}\equiv0\pmod n$ with $T-1\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-16a.title: Auxiliary identity, then Bézout
pumac-2015-power-16a.body:
All $c_n$ are positive rationals. Put $T_n=c_n^2+c_{n-2}c_{n+2}$ and $\lambda_n=2$ ($n$ even), $3$ ($n$ odd).

**Claim 1: $c_{n-3}T_n=c_{n+1}T_{n-2}$ for $n\ge4$.** Using the recurrences $c_{n+2}c_{n-3}=c_{n+1}c_{n-2}+c_nc_{n-1}$ and $c_{n+1}c_{n-4}=c_nc_{n-3}+c_{n-1}c_{n-2}$:
$$c_{n-3}T_n=c_{n-3}c_n^2+c_{n-2}(c_{n+1}c_{n-2}+c_nc_{n-1})=c_{n-3}c_n^2+c_{n-2}^2c_{n+1}+c_nc_{n-1}c_{n-2},$$
$$c_{n+1}T_{n-2}=c_{n+1}c_{n-2}^2+c_n(c_nc_{n-3}+c_{n-1}c_{n-2})=c_{n+1}c_{n-2}^2+c_n^2c_{n-3}+c_nc_{n-1}c_{n-2},$$
which agree.

**Claim 2: $T_n=\lambda_nc_{n-1}c_{n+1}$ for $n\ge2$.** $T_2=1+c_0c_4=2=2c_1c_3$ and $T_3=1+c_1c_5=3=3c_2c_4$ ($c_5=2$). If it holds for $n-2$, then by Claim 1 $c_{n-3}T_n=c_{n+1}\lambda_nc_{n-3}c_{n-1}$, so $T_n=\lambda_nc_{n-1}c_{n+1}$.

**Induction for integrality and coprimality.** Suppose $c_0,\dots,c_{m-1}$ ($m\ge5$) are integers with $\gcd(c_k,c_{k-1})=1$. By the recurrence $c_mc_{m-5}=c_{m-1}c_{m-4}+c_{m-2}c_{m-3}\in\mathbb Z$, and by Claim 2 at $n=m-2$: $c_mc_{m-4}=\lambda_{m-2}c_{m-1}c_{m-3}-c_{m-2}^2\in\mathbb Z$. As $\gcd(c_{m-4},c_{m-5})=1$, Bézout gives $c_m\in\mathbb Z$.
Adjacent coprimality of $c_m$: if a prime $p\mid c_m,c_{m-1}$, then from the first relation $p\mid c_{m-2}c_{m-3}$; $p\nmid c_{m-2}$ (as $\gcd(c_{m-1},c_{m-2})=1$), so $p\mid c_{m-3}$; then the second relation gives $p\mid c_{m-2}^2$, contradiction. (Base: $c_0,\dots,c_4$ are all $1$.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-16b.title: Invariant, key identity, induction
pumac-2015-power-16b.body:
For $k\ge0$ define $H_k$ in terms of $(a,b,c,e)=(d_k,d_{k+1},d_{k+2},d_{k+3})$ by
$$H_k=\begin{cases}b^2c^2-3a^2e^2-ac^3-b^3e&k\equiv0\pmod 3,\\ 3b^2c^2-a^2e^2-3ac^3-b^3e&k\equiv1,\\ 3b^2c^2-a^2e^2-ac^3-3b^3e&k\equiv2.\end{cases}$$

**Step 1: $H_k=0$ for all $k$.** Direct check: $H_0=4-27-1+24=0$ for $(1,2,1,-3)$, and $H_1,H_2$ vanish for $(2,1,-3,-7)$ and $(1,-3,-7,-17)$. For the step put $a=d_k$, $(b,c,e)=(d_{k+1},d_{k+2},d_{k+3})$ and $d_{k+4}=\frac{eb-\kappa_{k+4}c^2}{a}$ (recurrence at index $k+4$). A direct expansion (done for each residue of $k$ modulo $3$) gives the polynomial identity
$$a^2\,H_{k+1}\Bigl(b,c,e,\tfrac{eb-\kappa_{k+4}c^2}a\Bigr)=(eb-\kappa_{k+4}c^2)\,H_k(a,b,c,e),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad d_k\,H_{k+1}=d_{k+4}\,H_k.$$
As $d_k\ne0$, $H_k=0\Rightarrow H_{k+1}=0$. **Step 2: key identity $s_n:=d_nd_{n+5}-d_{n+2}d_{n+3}=\kappa_n\,d_{n+1}d_{n+4}$.** From the recurrences at indices $n+5$ and $n+4$: $d_{n+1}d_{n+5}=d_{n+4}d_{n+2}-\kappa_{n+5}d_{n+3}^2$ and $d_nd_{n+4}=d_{n+3}d_{n+1}-\kappa_{n+4}d_{n+2}^2$. Hence
$$d_{n+1}s_n=d_n(d_{n+4}d_{n+2}-\kappa_{n+5}d_{n+3}^2)-d_{n+1}d_{n+2}d_{n+3}=-\kappa_{n+4}d_{n+2}^3-\kappa_{n+5}d_nd_{n+3}^2 .$$
The claim is $d_{n+1}s_n=\kappa_nd_{n+1}^2d_{n+4}$. Multiplying by $d_n$ and using $d_nd_{n+4}=d_{n+3}d_{n+1}-\kappa_{n+4}d_{n+2}^2$, the claim is equivalent to
$$\kappa_nd_{n+1}^3d_{n+3}-\kappa_n\kappa_{n+4}d_{n+1}^2d_{n+2}^2+\kappa_{n+4}d_nd_{n+2}^3+\kappa_{n+5}d_n^2d_{n+3}^2=0,$$
and using the table $(\kappa_n,\kappa_{n+4},\kappa_{n+5})=(1,1,3),(1,3,1),(3,1,1)$ for $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$, this is exactly $-H_n=0$. So Step 1 gives the identity (for $d_{n+1}\ne0$).

**Step 3: adjacent terms are coprime and all $d_n$ are integers.** Base: $d_0,\dots,d_5=1,2,1,-3,-7,-17$ are integers with $\gcd(d_k,d_{k+1})=1$. Let $m\ge5$ and assume $d_0,\dots,d_{m-1}$ are integers with adjacent terms coprime.
*Integrality:* by Step 2, $d_md_{m-5}=d_{m-3}d_{m-2}+\kappa_{m-5}d_{m-4}d_{m-1}\in\mathbb Z$ and by the recurrence $d_md_{m-4}=d_{m-1}d_{m-3}-\kappa_md_{m-2}^2\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\gcd(d_{m-4},d_{m-5})=1$, Bézout gives $d_m\in\mathbb Z$.
*Coprimality of $d_m,d_{m-1}$:* let a prime $p$ divide both. The recurrence gives $p\mid\kappa_md_{m-2}^2$. If $p\mid d_{m-2}$ this contradicts $\gcd(d_{m-1},d_{m-2})=1$; so $p=3$, $\kappa_m=3$ and $3\nmid d_{m-2}$. The identity $d_md_{m-5}=d_{m-3}d_{m-2}+\kappa_{m-5}d_{m-4}d_{m-1}$ shows $3\mid d_{m-3}d_{m-2}$, hence $3\mid d_{m-3}$. The recurrence at index $m-1$, $d_{m-1}d_{m-5}=d_{m-2}d_{m-4}-\kappa_{m-1}d_{m-3}^2$, then gives $3\mid d_{m-2}d_{m-4}$, so $3\mid d_{m-4}$, contradicting $\gcd(d_{m-3},d_{m-4})=1$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-18.title: Reduction of $(2n-3)P$
pumac-2015-power-18.body:
By 4.6, for $n\ge2$, $(2n-3)P=\bigl(\frac{f}{a_n^2},\frac g{a_n^3}\bigr)$ with $f=a_n^2-a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$ and $g=a_{n-1}^2a_{n+2}-2a_{n-1}a_na_{n+1}$. By 5.2, $a_n$ is coprime to $a_{n\pm1},a_{n\pm2}$, so $f\equiv-a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$ and $g\equiv a_{n-1}^2a_{n+2}\pmod{a_n}$ are coprime to $a_n$: both coordinates are in lowest terms. The reduction recipe gives projective coordinates $(f\,a_n^3:g\,a_n^2:a_n^5)$; dividing by $a_n^2$ (in the sense of prime powers of $p$) gives $(fa_n:g:a_n^3)$. Hence:

* if $p\mid a_n$, this is $(0:g:0)$ with $p\nmid g$, i.e. $O=(0:1:0)$ in $E(\mathbb F_p)$;
* if $p\nmid a_n$, the $Z$-coordinate is nonzero, so the reduction is not $O$.

So $(2n-3)P\equiv O\pmod p\iff p\mid a_n$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $p\mid a_n$ for some $n$ (necessarily $n\ge4$ as $a_0=\dots=a_3=1$), then $(2n-3)P=O$ in $E(\mathbb F_p)$, so the order of $P$ divides the odd number $2n-3$: it is odd.
($\Leftarrow$) If $P$ has odd order $r$ in $E(\mathbb F_p)$, then $r\ge3$ ($P\ne O$, and $r=1$ would mean $P=O$), so $n=\frac{r+3}2\ge3$ is an integer with $(2n-3)P=rP=O$ in $E(\mathbb F_p)$, whence $p\mid a_n$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-19.title: Check the axioms
pumac-2015-power-19.body: $(A,+)$ is the trivial abelian group ($0$ is the identity and its own inverse; associativity and commutativity are trivial). Multiplication is closed, commutative and associative ($0\cdot0=0$). Distributivity: $0\cdot(0+0)=0=0\cdot0+0\cdot0$. The element $0$ is a multiplicative identity: $0\cdot0=0$. So all axioms hold and $A$ **is a ring** (the zero ring, in which $1=0$). It is not a field, because fields require $1\ne0$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-20a.title: Reduce powers
pumac-2015-power-20a.body: Every element of $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$ is $\sum_{i=0}^nc_i(\sqrt2)^i$ with $c_i\in\mathbb Q$. Since $(\sqrt2)^{2j}=2^j$ and $(\sqrt2)^{2j+1}=2^j\sqrt2$, grouping even and odd powers gives $\bigl(\sum_jc_{2j}2^j\bigr)+\bigl(\sum_jc_{2j+1}2^j\bigr)\sqrt2=a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. Conversely $a+b\sqrt2$ is the case $n=1$. So the sets are equal. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-20d.title: $\sqrt3\notin\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$
pumac-2015-power-20d.body: By part (a), $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]=\{a+b\sqrt2\}$. Suppose $\sqrt3=a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. Squaring: $3=a^2+2b^2+2ab\sqrt2$, so $ab=0$ ($\sqrt2$ is irrational). If $b=0$ then $a^2=3$; if $a=0$ then $2b^2=3$; neither has a rational solution. Hence $\sqrt3\notin\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$ and the fields are not equivalent. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-21b.title: The four automorphisms
pumac-2015-power-21b.body:
Let $\alpha=2\sqrt5+\sqrt{15}$ and $\beta=2\sqrt5-\sqrt{15}$; the roots are $\alpha,-\alpha,\beta,-\beta$. $f$ is irreducible ($\alpha^2=35+20\sqrt3$ generates $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ of degree $2$ and $\alpha=\sqrt5(2+\sqrt3)\notin\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$), so $K=\mathbb Q(\alpha)=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5,\sqrt3)$ has degree $4$ (note $\beta=\sqrt5(2-\sqrt3)\in K$, so $K$ contains all roots). An automorphism is determined by $\sqrt5\mapsto\pm\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt3\mapsto\pm\sqrt3$, giving:

* $\sigma_1$: $\sqrt5\mapsto\sqrt5$, $\sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3$ (identity): $\alpha\mapsto\alpha$, $\beta\mapsto\beta$.
* $\sigma_2$: $\sqrt5\mapsto\sqrt5$, $\sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3$: $\alpha\mapsto\beta$, $\beta\mapsto\alpha$, $-\alpha\mapsto-\beta$, $-\beta\mapsto-\alpha$.
* $\sigma_3$: $\sqrt5\mapsto-\sqrt5$, $\sqrt3\mapsto\sqrt3$: $\alpha\mapsto-\alpha$, $\beta\mapsto-\beta$.
* $\sigma_4$: $\sqrt5\mapsto-\sqrt5$, $\sqrt3\mapsto-\sqrt3$: $\alpha\mapsto-\beta$, $\beta\mapsto-\alpha$.

Each fixes $\mathbb Q$, respects sums and products (it is a field automorphism of $K$), and permutes the four roots of $f$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-22b.title: Count by valuation
pumac-2015-power-22b.body:
Clearly $\alpha\beta\equiv c$ forces $ab\equiv c\pmod2$, so the count is $0$ if $ab\not\equiv c$.

**One of $a,b$ nonzero (and $ab\equiv c$).** Say $a=1$, so $\alpha$ is odd (the case $b=1$ is symmetric). There are $2^{n-1}$ odd residues $\alpha$; then $\beta\equiv c\alpha^{-1}\pmod{2^n}$ is forced, and $\beta\equiv c\equiv ab=b\pmod2$ holds automatically. So the count is $2^{n-1}$. (The printed second case reads "$ab\equiv0$", but the condition must be $ab\equiv c\pmod 2$: for $a=b=c=1$ the count is also $2^{n-1}$ by the same argument, and the cases are otherwise exhaustive.)

**$a=b=c=0$, $c\not\equiv0\pmod{2^n}$.** Let $v=v_2(c)\in[1,n-1]$. Both $\alpha,\beta$ are even. Write $i=v_2(\alpha)\in[1,n]$ ($\alpha=0$ gives $\alpha\beta=0\ne c$, so $i\le n-1$), $\alpha=2^i\alpha'$ with $\alpha'$ odd. The congruence $2^i\alpha'\beta\equiv c\pmod{2^n}$ requires $2^i\mid c$, i.e. $i\le v$, and is then equivalent to $\beta\equiv\frac c{2^i}\alpha'^{-1}\pmod{2^{n-i}}$, which has $2^i$ solutions $\beta$ mod $2^n$. For $i=v$ the right side is odd, so $\beta$ is odd, not allowed. For $1\le i\le v-1$, $\beta$ is even automatically. The number of $\alpha$ with $v_2(\alpha)=i$ is $2^{n-i-1}$, so each $i$ contributes $2^{n-i-1}\cdot2^i=2^{n-1}$, for a total of $(v-1)2^{n-1}$.

**$a=b=c=0$, $c\equiv0\pmod{2^n}$.** We need $\alpha,\beta$ even with $v_2(\alpha)+v_2(\beta)\ge n$ (with $v_2(0)=n$). For $\alpha=0$: any even $\beta$, $2^{n-1}$ choices. For $v_2(\alpha)=i\in[1,n-1]$ ($2^{n-i-1}$ such $\alpha$): $\beta\equiv0\pmod{2^{n-i}}$, i.e. $2^i$ values (all even since $n-i\ge1$): $2^{n-1}$ per $i$. Total $2^{n-1}+(n-1)2^{n-1}=n2^{n-1}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-22c.title: Hensel-type counting
pumac-2015-power-22c.body:
**$k=1$.** We need $M\in GL_2(\mathbb F_2)$ with $\det(M-I)=1$, i.e. $M$ and $M-I$ both invertible: no eigenvalue $0$ or $1$. Among the $6$ elements of $GL_2(\mathbb F_2)$ these are the two elements of order $3$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. So the count is $2$.

**$k\ge2$.** Let $N=M-I$. The condition is $\det N\equiv2^{k-1}\pmod{2^k}$ (the only residue $\ne0$ divisible by $2^{k-1}$), and $M$ is invertible iff $\det(N+I)=1+\operatorname{tr}N+\det N$ is odd, i.e. (as $\det N$ is even) iff $\operatorname{tr}N$ is even. Let $C(k)$ be the number of such $N\in M_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)$.

*Lemma.* Let $N_0\in M_2(\mathbb F_2)$, $N_0\ne0$, $t\in\mathbb Z$ with $\det N_0\equiv t\pmod2$. For $j\ge1$ the number of $N\in M_2(\mathbb Z/2^j)$ with $N\equiv N_0\pmod2$ and $\det N\equiv t\pmod{2^j}$ is $8^{j-1}$.
*Proof.* Induct on $j$ ($j=1$: only $N_0$). Given a solution $N$ mod $2^j$ ($j\ge1$), its lifts mod $2^{j+1}$ are $N+2^jX$, $X\in M_2(\mathbb F_2)$ ($16$ of them), and $\det(N+2^jX)\equiv\det N+2^j(\delta x_{11}-\gamma x_{12}-\beta x_{21}+\alpha x_{22})\pmod{2^{j+1}}$ (since $2^{2j}\equiv0$). The linear form has coefficients $(\delta,\gamma,\beta,\alpha)\bmod2$, not all $0$ as $N\not\equiv0\pmod2$, so exactly $8$ of the $16$ choices of $X$ give $\det\equiv t\pmod{2^{j+1}}$. $\square$

Now split by $N\bmod2$. For $k\ge2$ we need $\det N\equiv0$ and $\operatorname{tr}N\equiv0\pmod 2$: the matrices over $\mathbb F_2$ with $\det=\operatorname{tr}=0$ are $0$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Each of the three nonzero ones contributes $8^{k-1}$ by the Lemma (with $t=2^{k-1}\equiv0$). For $N\equiv0\pmod2$ write $N=2N'$, $N'\in M_2(\mathbb Z/2^{k-1})$: then $\det N=4\det N'\equiv2^{k-1}\pmod{2^k}$, which is impossible for $k=2$ and for $k\ge3$ means $\det N'\equiv2^{k-3}\pmod{2^{k-2}}$; the number of such $N'$ is $16\,E(k-2)$, where $E(m)$ is the number of $N\in M_2(\mathbb Z/2^m)$ with $\det N\equiv2^{m-1}\pmod{2^m}$ (each class mod $2^{k-2}$ has $16$ lifts mod $2^{k-1}$). Hence
$$C(k)=3\cdot8^{k-1}+16E(k-2)\quad(k\ge3),\qquad C(2)=3\cdot 8=24.$$
The same method (no trace condition) gives $E(1)=6$ (the invertible matrices over $\mathbb F_2$), $E(2)=9\cdot8=72$ and $E(m)=9\cdot8^{m-1}+16E(m-2)$ for $m\ge3$ (the nonzero singular matrices over $\mathbb F_2$ number $10-1=9$). The solution of this recursion with these initial values is $E(m)=3\cdot2^{3m-1}-3\cdot2^{2m-1}$ (check: it satisfies the recursion because $\tfrac32 8^m=9\cdot8^{m-1}+16\cdot\tfrac32 8^{m-2}$ and $4^m=16\cdot4^{m-2}$, and matches $m=1,2$). Therefore, for $k\ge3$,
$$C(k)=3\cdot2^{3k-3}+16\bigl(3\cdot2^{3k-7}-3\cdot2^{2k-5}\bigr)=3\cdot2^{3k-3}+3\cdot2^{3k-3}-3\cdot2^{2k-1}=3\cdot2^{3k-2}-3\cdot2^{2k-1},$$
and for $k=2$: $24=3\cdot2^4-3\cdot2^3$ also fits. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2015-power-22d.title: Sum over $r=v_2(\det(M-I))$
pumac-2015-power-22d.body:
$|AGL_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)|=2^{2k}\,|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)|$ and $|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)|=6\cdot16^{k-1}$ (invertible matrices over $\mathbb Z/2^k$ reduce to the $6$ elements of $GL_2(\mathbb F_2)$, each with $2^{4(k-1)}$ lifts). For fixed $M$, the number of ruminative $(\vec v,M)$ is $|\mathrm{col}(M-I)|$, so
$$\mathrm{ratio}_k=\frac1{|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)|}\sum_M\frac{|\mathrm{col}(M-I)|}{2^{2k}}.$$
For $M$ with $r=v_2(\det(M-I))<k$ the summand is $2^{-r}$ (Proposition 39); for the remaining $M$ (with $\det(M-I)\equiv0\pmod{2^k}$) it is between $0$ and $1$.

The proportion of $M\in GL_2(\mathbb Z/2^k)$ with $v_2(\det(M-I))=r$ ($r\le k-1$) depends only on $M\bmod2^{r+1}$ and equals $p_r:=c(r+1)/|GL_2(\mathbb Z/2^{r+1})|$, where $c(j)$ is the count of part (c). So $p_0=\frac26=\frac13$ and, for $j=r+1\ge2$,
$$p_r=\frac{3\cdot2^{3j-2}-3\cdot2^{2j-1}}{6\cdot2^{4j-4}}=2^{-j+1}-2^{-2j+2}.$$
Then $\sum_{r\ge0}p_r=\frac13+\sum_{j\ge2}2^{-j+1}-4\sum_{j\ge2}4^{-j}=\frac13+1-\frac13=1$. Hence the proportion $q_k=1-\sum_{r<k}p_r$ of "exceptional" $M$ tends to $0$, and
$$\sum_{r<k}p_r2^{-r}\ \le\ \mathrm{ratio}_k\ \le\ \sum_{r<k}p_r2^{-r}+q_k.$$
Letting $k\to\infty$: $\lim\mathrm{ratio}_k=\sum_{r\ge0}p_r2^{-r}$, and
$$p_r2^{-r}=\bigl(2^{-j+1}-2^{-2j+2}\bigr)2^{-j+1}=2^{-2j+2}-2^{-3j+3}\ (j=r+1\ge2),\quad
\sum_{j\ge2}\bigl(4\cdot4^{-j}-8\cdot8^{-j}\bigr)=\frac13-\frac17=\frac4{21}.$$
Therefore the density is $\frac13+\frac4{21}=\frac{7+4}{21}=\frac{11}{21}$. $\blacksquare$
